articles.title: Tech Giants Face Earnings Pressure Amid Trade Tensions (AAPL)
articles.summary: Major tech companies, including Microsoft, Apple, Meta Platforms, and Amazon, are set to release their quarterly earnings amidst escalating trade tensions. Analysts expect a 15% average profit growth for these companies by 2025, but any earnings miss could lead to further sell-offs. Investors will scrutinize spending plans, particularly Microsoft's decision to halt some data center projects, and Apple's vulnerability to tariffs. However, Apple's increased demand from consumers purchasing ahead of price hikes might offset its tariff risks. Amazon's e-commerce and advertising segments face tariff risks, but its high-margin web services could cushion impacts. Executives are unlikely to provide reliable forecasts due to economic uncertainties, but tech giants' strong market positions and balance sheets might help them withstand downturns, making them attractive to bargain hunters if trade tensions ease.

articles.title: Apple (AAPL) Faces Price Target Cut Amid Tariff Concerns | AAPL
articles.summary: Raymond James has reduced its price target for Apple (AAPL) from $250 to $230 due to concerns over tariffs. The firm believes that Apple may increase product prices in the U.S., potentially leading to reduced demand and decreased earnings. Currently, Apple can meet about half of U.S. iPhone demand with manufacturing outside of China, but it's uncertain whether imports from countries like India will benefit from tariff exemptions. According to 44 analysts, the average one-year price target for Apple is $236.26, with a potential upside of 11.86% from the current price of $211.21. The consensus recommendation from 50 brokerage firms is 'Outperform' with an average rating of 2.1, indicating a strong buy. GuruFocus estimates the fair value of Apple in one year to be $205.84, suggesting a downside of 2.54% from the current price.

articles.title: Tariffs will likely raise much less money than White House projects, economists say | The Great Southern Herald
articles.summary: Economists expect the Trump administration's tariff policy to generate significantly less revenue than the White House projects. According to White House trade adviser Peter Navarro, tariffs would raise about $US600 billion ($950.3b) a year and $US6 trillion ($9.5t) over a decade. However, economists such as Mark Zandi, chief economist at Moody's, and Ernie Tedeschi, director of economics at the Yale Budget Lab, estimate that the total revenue would be less than half of Navarro's projection, ranging from $US100b to $US200b ($316.7b) a year. The economists argue that the revenue estimate must account for the many economic impacts of tariffs, including reduced economic activity, lower demand, and retaliation from other countries. They also point out that a 20 per cent broad tariff would raise about $US250b ($396b) a year, while a 50 per cent across-the-board tariff would raise about $US780b ($1.2t) per year. However, even this higher estimate does not account for lower US economic growth due to retaliation or the negative growth effects from the tariffs themselves. The economists warn that tariffs would have a negative impact on the US economy, leading to a recession and undermining the fiscal situation. They also note that the tariffs will likely have a short life span and may be undone easily by a future president. The revenue from tariffs will be crucial in offsetting the cost of passing a package of tax cuts, and economists warn that if tariffs don't cover the full cost, Republican lawmakers would have to find cuts elsewhere or increase the nation's debt. 'There's zero probability these tariffs will last for 10 years,' Zandi said. 'If they last until next year I'd be very surprised.'

articles.title: Jim Cramer Says Washington Doesn't 'Care' About Apple (AAPL) $500 Billion Investment, Services Jobs
articles.summary: Despite market optimism after President Trump's indication of possible talks with China, Wall Street analysts are warning about recession risks due to tariffs and declining consumer sentiment. Adam Parker, CEO of Trivariate Research, believes that earnings reports will show an economic slowdown, stating, 'You know there's a difference between a growth scare and an actual growth slowdown... I think in this case it is a growth slowdown.' Jim Cramer, on CNBC, expressed concerns about Apple Inc.'s (AAPL) $500 billion investment and services jobs, saying that the government doesn't 'care' about the company's contributions, despite creating 'millions' of services jobs and investing heavily in the US. The company is impacted by President Trump's tariffs.
